- The income tax is California's largest tax and pays for most of the General Fund, the account used for most public services. The state plans to spend about $250 billion from it this year.

**Prop. 3: Summary**

**What it does**
- Would permanently extend California's income tax on high earners, which voters first approved in 2012 and renewed in 2016. It is set to expire in 2031.
- Applies to individuals earning more than $371,000 and couples earning more than $743,000 a year.
- Top earners would keep paying a 12.3% rate. With the state's existing 1% surcharge on income over $1 million for mental health services, the combined rate would be 13.3%, the highest in the nation.

**Fiscal impact**
- The tax has brought in between $5 billion and $15 billion a year. Revenue swings with the stock market, interest rates, and other factors affecting top earners' income.
- Most of the money would flow through Proposition 98, which sets aside about 40% of the state budget for K-12 schools and community colleges. Of that money, 89% goes to K-12 and 11% to community colleges. Excess revenue above a certain level would go to a rainy day fund.
- The Legislative Analyst's Office says the measure frees up general funds that would otherwise go to schools, which can then pay for healthcare and other services.
- In strong revenue years, the tax covers about 15% of the state's K-12 budget. Supporters say that without it, districts could lay off up to 50,000 teachers.

**Relation to the billionaire tax**
- The article does not directly call Prop. 40 a "billionaire tax," but it describes Prop. 40 as a 5% tax on Californians with more than $1 billion in assets. A linked article refers to a "billionaire tax" on the November ballot, which is likely the same measure.
- Prop. 40 would send 90% of its revenue to healthcare, with the rest split among schools, food assistance, and other services.
- The California Teachers Association opposes Prop. 40, arguing schools would get too little. The union says it is not campaigning against Prop. 40 and is focusing on Prop. 3.

**Supporters**
- The California Teachers Association, the state's largest teachers union, is the primary backer. Its president, David Goldberg, says the measure is vital for schools.
- The union gathered signatures to qualify the measure and knocked on more than 200,000 doors.
- The union says it began the process more than four years before expiration so schools can plan budgets well in advance.
- Children Now, an advocacy group, argues that California's large student-to-teacher ratios and achievement gap require more school funding. Its policy adviser, Rob Manwaring, also warns that federal cuts and a possible downturn could squeeze budgets.

**Opponents**
- Taxpayer groups oppose the measure. Susan Shelley of the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association questions whether schools need more money given recent funding increases and declining enrollment.
- She argues that some districts have costly labor contracts and that the current situation is unsustainable.

**Money raised**
- Supporters, led by the teachers union and other groups, have raised more than $40 million.
- Opponents, including taxpayer associations, have raised $5,500.
- The article does not name any major individual or organizational donors.

**Arguments for**
- The tax targets only the wealthiest Californians while funding schools and services.
- Stable, long-term funding helps schools plan.
- California has one of the highest student-to-teacher ratios in the country: 1 teacher per 22 students in 2022–23, versus a national average of 1:15.
- Federal cuts and possible economic downturns may require more state revenue.

- Enrollment has dropped by more than 500,000 students since the mid-2010s, so schools may not need more money.

**Polling**
- A September Public Policy Institute of California poll found 58% of likely voters planned to vote yes.
- Among Democrats, 82% supported the measure. Among Republicans, 18% did.

**SPUR's Analysis of Prop 3 (High-Earner Income Tax Extension)**

SPUR recommends a **YES** vote.

**What Prop. 3 does**
- Makes permanent the state's marginal income tax rates on the top 2% of earners (10.3%, 11.3%, and 12.3%). These rates have applied since 2012 and are set to expire in 2030.
- Revenue would mainly fund K–12 schools and community colleges under Proposition 98. About 40% ($2 billion to $6 billion a year) would go to education. The rest could support children's healthcare, the rainy day fund, and other General Fund uses.
- If the rates expire, the state would lose an estimated $5 billion to $15 billion a year.

**SPUR's reasoning**
- The tax has generated more than $119 billion for education and healthcare since 2012, with no evidence that high earners have left California because of it.
- It is highly progressive, affecting only top earners, and supports programs like universal school meals that benefit low-income students.
- It would help backfill Medi-Cal as federal cuts from H.R. 1 threaten healthcare access.

**Revenue volatility**
- Recent annual revenue is about $9 billion to $10 billion, but it fluctuates with the economy and stock market. The LAO estimates a range of $5 billion to $15 billion.
- Capital-gains-linked income keeps revenue volatile. Any surplus would go to debt reduction and the rainy day fund, which SPUR says helps offset that volatility.

**High-earner migration**
- California has had the second-lowest out-migration rate among $200,000-plus households of any state over the past decade.
- Less-educated and lower-income adults have left the state faster, which SPUR attributes to affordability and cost-of-living concerns.

**State budget effects**
- Prop. 98 sets a minimum level of education funding. Because this tax counts toward that minimum, it frees General Fund dollars for other programs.
- If the tax expires, the state would need other General Fund revenue to meet education requirements in the short term. Over time, the Prop. 98 minimum could decline depending on the formula, economic conditions, and legislative decisions.

**Trade-offs and criticisms SPUR raises**
- Permanence would limit future tax flexibility.
- Reliance on top earners would increase budget volatility.
- The measure is restrictive, since the Prop. 98 minimum must be met before funds can be allocated more flexibly.

**Equity**
- SPUR argues that letting the tax expire would cut education spending that disproportionately affects low-income students and students of color.
- Up to $2 billion a year for Medi-Cal would mostly serve low-income people and people of color.

**Note:** This page is SPUR's own endorsement. It doesn't present detailed arguments from opponents, so the case against Prop. 3 isn't represented here.

**Type:** Initiative constitutional amendment, placed on the ballot by petition signatures.

**Question:** Should the income tax rates on high earners, passed by voters in 2012 and extended in 2016, be made permanent?

## What It Does
- Makes permanent the 2012 income tax rates for high earners, which are currently set to expire in 2031.
- Creates no new taxes.
- Affects only individuals with incomes above $371,000 a year. The threshold is higher for married couples and heads of household.
- Background: 2012's Prop 30 created the higher brackets, and 2016 voters extended them through 2030. The page gives both 2030 and 2031 as the expiration year.

## Fiscal Impact
- Estimated revenue of $5 billion to $15 billion per year, which varies with the economy.
- About 40% of revenue typically goes to K-12 schools and community colleges.
- A smaller portion goes to state reserves to help balance the budget during economic downturns.
- Remaining funds could support other state programs, such as low-income healthcare.
- Under current law, revenue goes to the Education Protection Account, with some going to the General Fund for reserves and low-income healthcare.

- Supporters say the measure has accountability provisions guaranteeing funds go directly to local schools. The page does not describe these provisions.

- The measure only extends existing rates on the wealthiest 2% of Californians.
- It prevents billions in future cuts to schools and healthcare.
- It includes accountability measures to route funds to local schools.

- The measure turns temporary taxes into permanent, higher income taxes.
- California has a spending problem, not a revenue problem.
- Schools have declined since 2012 despite increased revenue.

**Varner and Young (2018, with Allen Prohofsky of the Franchise Tax Board)**

- Research on the question is growing rapidly, but no clear consensus has emerged.

- **Income tax:** The income tax is the state's largest tax and pays for most General Fund spending. Rates rise with income. For example, a married couple pays 1% on the first $21,000, 2% on income from $21,000 to $50,000, and 4% on income from $50,000 to $80,000.

**Prop 3 (California Children's Education and Health Care Protection Act of 2026): Summary of the Legal Text**

**Overview:** The measure amends Section 36 of Article XIII of the California Constitution. It keeps the existing income tax rates on high earners and removes their scheduled expiration, so the rates would no longer end in 2030.

**Tax rates and thresholds**
- The text sets higher rates on taxable income above certain levels, layered on the existing 9.3% rate. Single filers pay 10.3% on income above $250,000, 11.3% above $300,000, and 12.3% above $500,000.
- For the joint-filer schedule, the rates are 10.3% above $340,000, 11.3% above $408,000, and 12.3% above $680,000.
- Brackets are indexed for inflation starting in 2013.
- The sales tax increase in the same section expired January 1, 2017, and is not revived.

**Revenue allocation**
- **Education Protection Account (EPA):** Revenue goes into a General Fund account that is continuously appropriated. The Director of Finance estimates annual revenue, and the Controller makes quarterly transfers, with year-end true-ups.
- **89/11 split:** Eleven percent goes to community college districts through the Board of Governors. Eighty-nine percent goes to K-12 school districts, county offices of education, and charter schools through the Superintendent of Public Instruction. Minimums apply: $100 per full-time community college student and $200 per K-12 unit of average daily attendance.
- **Health care:** After the EPA covers the minimum funding guarantee and the workload budget, the Director of Finance identifies any remainder. Fifty percent of that remainder, capped at $2 billion per fiscal year, goes to the Department of Health Care Services for critical, emergency, acute, and preventive care for children and families. The text ties this to Medi-Cal and licensed providers.
- **Budget emergencies:** The health allocation can be suspended by statute during a declared budget emergency, but not by more than the proportional cut to overall General Fund spending. It cannot replace existing General Fund money and must be used to draw federal Medicaid matching funds.
- **Rainy Day Fund:** The operative text does not allocate money to the Rainy Day Fund. The findings say the measure helps build and sustain it. The text does treat EPA revenue as General Fund revenue for purposes of the state's reserve and minimum funding rules (Article XVI, Section 8).

**Audit and accountability**
- Each school entity must complete an annual independent financial and compliance audit that verifies proper use of EPA funds. Audit costs may be paid from the EPA and are not treated as administrative costs.
- The Controller may audit the Local Revenue Fund 2011 and must audit the EPA.
- The Attorney General or a local district attorney must investigate misuse and may seek civil or criminal penalties.
- Local governing boards must make EPA spending decisions in open session, cannot use EPA funds for administrator salaries or benefits or other administrative costs, and must publish annual accounting online.

- The page's markup does not clearly show new operative provisions. The findings describe the measure's purpose, but they are not operative law.

**Restrictions on future legislatures**
- EPA money is continuously appropriated and cannot pay for costs of the Legislature, the Governor, or other state agencies.
- EPA distributions to schools are self-executing and are not delayed by a failure to pass a budget or by other budget actions.
- The health allocation can be suspended only during a declared budget emergency, and only within the limits described above.
- Section 5 provides that if a competing income tax measure on the same ballot receives fewer votes, this measure prevails and the other is void.

**Abstract:** Using administrative income tax data, Rauh and Shyu study Proposition 30, a 2012 California ballot measure that raised marginal tax rates by up to 3 percentage points for high-income households. They examine how high earners responded.

**Main findings:**

- **Out-migration:** Relative to baseline departure rates for their income levels, an additional 0.8% of the residential tax base in the top bracket left California in 2013.
- **Behavioral response on the intensive margin:** Using matched out-of-state taxpayers as controls, they estimate an income elasticity with respect to the marginal net-of-tax rate of 2.5 to 3.2 for high earners who stayed.
- **Revenue erosion:** These responses offset 45.2% of the windfall state revenue within the first year and 60.9% within two years.
- **Extensive margin share:** Migration (the extensive margin) accounts for 9.5% of the total revenue erosion.

**Data:** The study uses California Franchise Tax Board administrative income tax data, with out-of-state taxpayers matched as controls. The authors also used TAXSIM, a tax calculator, with help from Daniel Feenberg.

**Prop 3** would make permanent the higher income tax rates on top earners. Voters approved these rates in 2012 and extended them in 2016. They apply to individuals earning about $371,000 and couples earning about $743,000 a year, and are set to expire in 2031.

- **Fiscal impact:** The rates generate roughly $10 billion a year.
- **Supporters:** Xavier Becerra (candidate for governor), the California Democratic Party, and the California Teachers Association.
- **Opponents:** The California Republican Party, the California Taxpayers Association, and the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association.
- **Campaign money:** Support totals $89.3 million, including $60.2 million from the California Teachers Association and $7.5 million from the National Education Association. Opposition totals about $5.5 thousand.
- **Newsom and Hilton:** The guide does not say whether Governor Newsom or Hilton has taken a position.

**Arguments for:** Supporters say the rates are "the cornerstone of California's progressive tax system." They note that the number of Californians subject to the rates has more than doubled since 2012, and that letting them expire would cut funding for schools and health care.

**Arguments against:** Opponents say voters were told in 2012 the rates were temporary, to stabilize the budget after the Great Recession. They argue that making them permanent, even when the state has plenty of money, risks driving top earners to lower-tax states. They say the state should cut spending first.

**Volatility and migration:** The guide raises high-earner migration only as an opposition concern. It does not analyze revenue volatility directly, though the opposition's point about making the rates permanent in flush years implies that revenue depends on economic conditions.

**Author:** Robert Gutierrez, president of the California Taxpayers Association. CalMatters published this as a guest commentary in its California Voices forum in August 2026, and its editor's note describes him as an anti-tax advocate.

**Position:** He opposes Proposition 3, which would make permanent the high-income tax first approved in 2012, and urges voters to reject it.

**Main arguments and claims:**
- **Pattern of extensions:** He argues temporary tax increases tend to stay. Voters were told the 2012 increase was a short-term emergency fix, then were asked to extend it in 2016.
- **Cost of living:** He cites a PPIC poll finding that about half of Californians name cost of living as their top concern, and that 55% prefer lower taxes and fewer services.
- **Spending baseline:** Once government budgets around higher revenue, he says, officials treat that level as the starting point.
- **Small businesses:** Many pass-through businesses report income on personal returns, so he argues higher rates would raise their costs and, in turn, customer prices.
- **Tax burden:** He says California has the nation's highest personal income taxes, the highest state sales tax and gas tax, and an extra 1.3% tax on wages for State Disability Insurance.
- **Revenue volatility:** He argues high earners are the state's most volatile revenue source, so permanent commitments tied to them reduce flexibility in downturns.

I'm not going to give you a bare yes or no. This is a contested tax measure, and the disagreement is mostly about values. The question is how much weight to give stable school and health funding versus keeping top tax rates from becoming permanent. I can't settle that for you, but I did the research, and here is the short version.

**What it does**
- **Rates:** A Yes makes the Prop 30 (2012) and Prop 55 (2016) top income tax rates permanent. Those are 10.3% to 12.3% on income above about $371k for single filers and $743k for joint filers. If it fails, they expire in 2031 and revert to 9.3% ([LAist](https://laist.com/news/politics/voter-guides/2026-election-california-general-proposition-3-income-tax)). It creates no new rate.
- **Revenue:** The Legislative Analyst's Office (LAO) estimates $5–15B a year, swinging with the stock market. The top 2% of taxpayers pay about half of state income tax. Roughly 40% of the revenue goes to schools and community colleges, and the rest goes to other programs and reserves ([LAO](https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=3&year=2026)).
- **Combined rate:** With the separate 1% mental-health surcharge on income over $1M, the top combined rate is 13.3%, the highest in the U.S. ([CalMatters](https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/10/prop-3-california/)).
- **Prop 40:** This is separate from the billionaire tax on the same ballot.

**Strongest case for Yes**
- **Budget hole:** It extends an existing tax. If the rates lapse, top earners get a rate cut and the state loses $5–15B a year. In May, the administration and LAO already projected structural deficits of roughly $10–14B a year with the tax in place ([LAO](https://lao.ca.gov/Publications/Report/5187)).
- **Migration:** The "they'll leave" worry may be overstated. Varner and Young estimate each 1-point rate increase after Prop 30 cost about 40 million-dollar earners to net migration ([CalMatters](https://calmatters.org/economy/2023/01/wealth-tax-migration/)).
- **Accountability:** School funds come with annual audits, open-session spending decisions, and no administrative spending ([legal text](https://growsf.org/voter-guide/san-francisco-voter-guide-november-2026-election/measures/prop-3/legal-text/)). Much of this may carry over from existing law, and I couldn't confirm which parts are new.

**Strongest case for No**
- **"Temporary" became permanent:** The 2012 increase was sold as lasting seven years, was extended 12 more in 2016, and would now have no end date ([ballot argument](https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/3/arguments-rebuttals.htm)). Undoing a constitutional amendment takes another statewide vote. A No isn't final either, since CalMatters notes the teachers union would get two more tries before expiration.
- **Volatile revenue:** LAO warned in May that the revenue boom rests heavily on AI-driven stock valuations. The May budget already uses roughly $20B in reserves.
- **Behavioral responses:** Rauh and Shyu estimate responses to Prop 30 erased about 45% of the expected new revenue in year one and 61% by year two. Only 9.5% of that came from people leaving ([NBER](https://www.nber.org/papers/w26349)). This conflicts with the Varner and Young findings, though both use state tax data.
- **Spending versus results:** Per-pupil spending is up 102% since 2013 versus 56% nationally, per Edunomics Lab figures cited in [CalMatters](https://calmatters.org/commentary/2025/02/california-school-grades-spending/). Test scores were flat or down over that period. The measure's rules govern how money is spent, not whether outcomes improve.

**Claims I'd discount**
- **Size of the school cut:** Sources disagree. The teachers union says 15%, CalMatters says the tax equals 3–10% of K-12 spending, and LAO says only about 40% of the lost revenue would come out of school funding. PolitiFact rated a similar [2016 Prop 55 ad](https://www.politifact.com/factchecks/2016/sep/13/yes-55/yes-55-school-claim-graded-mostly-false) "Mostly False."
- **"Health care" in the title:** The Budget Center says the Prop 55 Medi-Cal allocation has never actually sent money to Medi-Cal. The benefit is indirect, through freed-up General Fund dollars ([Budget Center](https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/should-voters-approve-prop-3-how-top-tax-rates-have-helped-californians/)).
- **Ballot arguments:** No state agency has fact-checked either side's arguments.

**How it maps to your vote**
- Yes fits if you want a durable dedicated revenue source for schools and Medi-Cal and accept permanent top rates and the volatility.
- No fits if you think California's rates and spending are already too high, want the sunset to force a re-vote, or doubt that more money is improving schools.

For context, not as a reason: the Yes side has raised about $89M against about $5,500 for the No side ([KQED](https://www.kqed.org/voterguide/california/proposition-3)). PPIC's October poll had it ahead 58–40 ([Yahoo/PPIC](https://www.yahoo.com/news/politics/articles/california-prop-3-tax-top-204145695.html)). Polls close at 8 p.m. today.

**Limits of my research:** I couldn't read the official PDFs, so the legal-text details come from an annotated copy. The per-pupil spending and test-score figures come from search summaries, not full articles. Thresholds, the sunset year, and revenue peaks vary slightly across sources. I also couldn't confirm Governor Newsom's position, because the sources conflicted. If you tell me which of these tradeoffs matters most to you, I can help you work out which way it points.
